reviews.title: This game cheats
reviews.text:
When you play against the computer on the “master” level, you notice inevitable patterns. One of them is that when you play the best possible word, a window pops up saying “You played the best word!” Immediately after that, the computer’s next word will be better than yours. Over fifty percent of the time, it will be twice as good as yours. This happens almost every single time. The statistical probability of this is close to zero. 

Another pattern is that when you post a seven-letter word, at least eighty percent of the time the computer will follow it immediately with its own seven-letter word. Again, this is exceedingly improbable in a randomized letter selection.

Another pattern is that the computer will often post three or more seven-letter words in a row. Sometimes, it will post a couple of seven-letter words, then a “normal” word, then a seven-letter word again.

Another pattern is that when you find yourself inevitably behind the computer in score and you battle back, the moment you reach or overtake the computer, it will hit you with a seven-letter word. This happens too often to be random.

Another pattern is that when you start off strong and have built a lead, the computer will give you a no-vowel rack. If you are able to use a couple of the consonants, the computer will replace them with other consonants until the computer overtakes your lead. Alternatively, it will give you an all-vowel rack.

Another pattern is that if you have letters that are difficult to play, and you play a few of them for low score, the computer will replace them with the very same letters.

When the computer gives you an all-vowel rack, it will contain three or four of the same vowels. If you have four Es, for example, and you play an E and an O, it will usually replace them with two Es, until your rack is simply unplayable.

Another pattern is that at least eighty percent of the time when you play a “normal” word and the computer follows with its own “normal” word, then computer’s word will be worth three or four points more than yours. It will do this consistently. If you play a 26-point word, for example, it will respond with a 29-point word. You then play a 34-point word followed by the computer’s 38-point word. You then come up with a 52-point word, so the computer answers with a 60-point word. And so forth.

Another pattern is that the computer will play bizarrely obscure words. When you highlight the word to find its definition, it will say “Alternate spelling of…” or it will be a transliteration of a foreign word. If you try playing an “alternate spelling” of any word, it will be rejected.

If you play a two-person game, and you play as both persons, none of these patterns arise. When two players are involved, the letter distribution looks random. When you play against the computer at “master” level, the computer stacks the deck against you.

reviews.title: Closest to Hasbro Scrabble
reviews.text:
Yes, I miss Hasbro Scrabble being online. I played it for so many years and I’ve never really found anything that comes close until I found Word Master.

You can choose the level of difficulty you want to play. It’s very easy. To navigate you can even choose different board shapes and as hesitant as I was being such a Hasbrouck fan, I do find that I like this one. And I know there’s a couple more out there that are popular but if you’re like a pro scrabble player sort of like me kinda lol you’re gonna like this give it a try.
